body_html:
Which t-shirt works best for an event or festival?

Event shirts have a short, intense life: they are handed out on the day, worn in the sun or the rain, washed a few times and then become a souvenir. That means three things matter more than anything else: a low price per piece, a full size range so nobody is left out, and a fabric that takes a print cleanly. The classic Fruit of the Loom tees tick all three, which is why they are a standard blank for runs, fundraisers, company days, weddings, conferences and festival crews across Europe.

Our {{LINK:blank-t-shirts|guide to blank t-shirts for printing}} compares the models in more depth.

How many event t-shirts should you order?

The most common mistake is ordering exactly one shirt per name on the list. People sign up late, sizes get swapped and a print can go wrong. A simple rule of thumb from event organisers:

  • Staff and volunteers: one shirt per person, plus 5–10 % spares in M, L and XL.
  • Participants (runs, tournaments): base the order on confirmed registrations at the cut-off date, plus approx. 5 % spares.
  • Giveaways and merch: start smaller than you think — leftover printed shirts cannot be returned. Reorders of the same model match the first batch.
  • Multi-day festivals: crew often need two shirts each, so they can wash one.

For a mixed adult group, M and L usually make up the largest share. Ask people for their size when they register and check the chest widths in our {{LINK:size-guide|Fruit of the Loom size guide}} — the classic tees are a regular unisex fit.

Which colours work for events?

The colour does more than look good on photos — it changes the print price and how easy your team is to spot:

  • Bright colours (red, yellow, royal blue) make staff and volunteers easy to find in a crowd. Choose one colour for crew and another for participants.
  • White and light colours are the cheapest to print with DTG and give the sharpest full-colour logos and sponsor prints.
  • Black and navy hide stains at outdoor events and look good on merch, but dark shirts need a white underbase, which usually costs a little more per piece.
  • Heather grey contains polyester; tell your printer so they choose the right ink and heat.

What does the print add per shirt?

The print usually costs about as much as the shirt itself, or more. These are typical net prices from public price lists of European print shops for 100 shirts (checked September 2026); your printer's quote will vary with colours, size and placement:

Screen printing gets cheaper per piece the more you order, because the set-up cost is shared. For small runs under approx. 30 shirts or many different names and numbers, DTF or vinyl is usually cheaper. Our {{LINK:printing|guide to printing on Fruit of the Loom}} explains the techniques, and {{LINK:price-per-100|what 100 Fruit of the Loom t-shirts cost}} has the full breakdown.

How far ahead should you order event t-shirts?

Work backwards from the event date. The blanks are the quick part: Marmalade Co. dispatches within 0–1 business day and DHL delivers in approx. 2–3 business days. The print shop is usually the bottleneck, especially in spring and early summer when every club and festival orders at once.

  1. 4–6 weeks before: fix the design, the shirt model and colour, and get a quote from your printer.
  2. 3–4 weeks before: close registrations or size lists and order the blanks.
  3. 2–3 weeks before: blanks arrive at the printer; approve the proof.
  4. 1 week before: printed shirts delivered, sorted by size and name.

Ask your printer for their current lead time before you promise a date — and add a buffer for proof changes.

Checklist for event t-shirts

  • Pick one model for everyone, so the fit and colour are identical.
  • Collect sizes at registration, not on the day.
  • Order 5–10 % spares in the middle sizes.
  • Give your printer the product code (e.g. 61-036) and the colour name.
  • Check sponsor logos are supplied as vector files.
  • Plan who hands out shirts and how they are sorted.

Organising a club season or a team instead of a one-off event? See our {{LINK:bulk-tshirts|guide to buying bulk t-shirts for printing}}.

faq.q: What is the cheapest t-shirt for an event?
faq.a: The Fruit of the Loom Valueweight T is one of the cheapest good-quality event shirts. At Marmalade Co. it costs €6.95, with 5 % off from 3 and 10 % off from 5 pieces, so 100 blank shirts come to approx. €632.50 including the €7 DHL fee, or approx. €6.33 per guest. Prices update weekly and VAT is included.

faq.q: How many spare event t-shirts should I order?
faq.a: Plan for approx. 5–10 % extra, mostly in sizes M, L and XL. Spares cover late sign-ups, size swaps and the odd misprint. For giveaways, start smaller than you think: printed shirts cannot be returned, and a reorder of the same Fruit of the Loom model will match the first batch in cut and colour.

faq.q: How far in advance should I order t-shirts for an event?
faq.a: Start four to six weeks before the event with the design and a print quote, and order the blanks three to four weeks before. Blanks from Marmalade Co. are dispatched within 0–1 business day and arrive in approx. 2–3 business days, so the print shop's lead time is usually what decides your schedule, especially in spring.

faq.q: Which print method is cheapest for event t-shirts?
faq.a: For 50 or more shirts with a one- or two-colour logo, screen printing is usually cheapest per piece because the set-up cost is shared, at approx. €2 per shirt for 100 pieces in one colour. For small runs, full-colour designs or individual names, DTF transfer or vinyl is often cheaper and needs no set-up.

faq.q: Can I mix sizes and colours and still get the quantity discount?
faq.a: Yes. At Marmalade Co. the 5 % and 10 % quantity discounts count all sizes and colours of the same product together. So 20 Valueweight T-shirts in five sizes and two colours still get 10 % off, and shipping is a flat €7 per order to 11 EU countries.
